entities.summary:
The Battle of Cynoscephalae was a pivotal clash between the Macedonian and Roman armies, fought on August 6, 197 BCE, in Thessaly, Greece. This decisive victory marked a turning point in the Second Macedonian War, as the Romans, led by Titus Quinctius Flamininus, defeated the Macedonians under King Philip V. The Roman triumph not only secured their control of the region but also paved the way for the eventual decline of Macedonian power and the rise of Rome as the dominant force in the Mediterranean.

The battle itself is notable for its innovative tactics, as the Romans employed a new formation, known as the 'oblique order,' which allowed them to outmaneuver the more traditional Macedonian phalanx. This tactical advantage proved crucial in the outcome, as the Romans were able to exploit the weaknesses of the Macedonian line and deliver a crushing blow.

The consequences of the Battle of Cynoscephalae were far-reaching, as it not only marked the beginning of Roman dominance in the region but also set the stage for the eventual conquest of Greece. The battle's impact can be seen in the subsequent decades, as Rome continued to expand its territories, incorporating much of the Hellenistic world into its vast empire.

As the Roman historian Polybius noted, 'the battle of Cynoscephalae was the beginning of the Roman supremacy in Greece.' This assessment highlights the significance of the battle, not only as a military victory but also as a turning point in the history of the Mediterranean world.
